name: Emeka Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an operator on line two at Hollins Bakery, the biscuit factory by the railway bridge. I run the flow wrapper, which seals the biscuits into those pillow packs, and the case packer after it. Most of my shift is chasing jams, changing film reels, tweaking the sealing temperature and getting the line back up before the shift lead shouts. I've been there five years, on rotating shifts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle. When the wrapper throws a fault code, I'll photograph it and ask an AI app what it means before maintenance even turns up, and half the time I've fixed it myself. I'm also doing an online course on PLCs, the little computers that control the line, on my days off. What wears me out is the night rota and the smell of sugar in my clothes. I share a flat with my cousin, so at least nobody minds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, at least to my friends. Online I'd say we dodged the bad side and the useful bits are still there. At work the older guys would tease me about my phone, and fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'm well paid for an operator, and there are bakeries and packaging plants all over this side of town. It'd just mean my plan to move into controls work takes the normal route, not a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: finish the PLC course by the summer, then apply for the junior controls technician job when it comes up at Hollins. I'd keep the app for fault codes. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're already learning about PLCs. Would you keep going with that in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Definitely. Lines still need people who understand what's going on inside the cabinet, whether or not AI takes off. A controls technician earns about a third more than I do, and nobody's going to robot that away in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your money? Anything you'd change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I've got about ten months of costs in savings and a small index fund. My cousin and I split rent, so my costs are low. I'd just keep at it.

say: To friends, the plateau would feel like a **let-down**.
Online I'd say we dodged the **bad side** and kept the useful bits.
think: I'd be **fine**: well paid, with plants all over this side of town.
My move into **controls work** would just take the normal route.
do: Finish the **PLC course** by summer and apply for the controls technician job.
Keep using the **AI app** to read fault codes.
Keep paying into the **index fund** monthly.
S0.quote: A controls technician earns about a third more than I do, and nobody's going to robot that away in this picture.
fieldNote: He already **uses AI daily** to diagnose machine faults before maintenance arrives.
His career plan, **operator to controls technician**, runs whatever happens with AI.
Low costs from **sharing a flat** give him a lot of room to move.

steps.text: Finish the online PLC course by summer
Keep reading wrapper fault codes with the AI app
Keep paying into the index fund every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for operators to get ahead of it, not hide from it. And I'd say the savings should be shared: if Hollins saves money, wages and training should go up. I'd post about the union pushing for a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. The office gets hit first, and robots come slowly to the floor, which gives me years to become the person who installs and fixes them. The guys who refuse to touch anything new are the ones I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course and then pay for a robot programming certificate myself, around eight hundred. I'd ask to shadow the integrator when Hollins brings in its first robot. I'd use AI to write up shift reports so I look like the guy who already gets it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, almost excited. I know that's not how most people would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talk about this as an opportunity. Who loses out at Hollins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen in purchasing, who orders the film and the cartons, and the two clerks in the shipping office. Their jobs are exactly the ones on your card. And probably Dev on line one, who's fifty-four and won't use the touchscreen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for automation yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I've already shown my shift lead a video of a cobot, a small robot arm that works next to people, stacking cases on a pallet. That's the worst job on our line. If it means nobody wrecks their back there, I'm for it, as long as nobody gets sacked.

say: Operators should **get ahead** of automation, not hide from it.
If Hollins saves money, **wages and training** should go up too.
think: The slow arrival of **robots** gives me years to become the person who fixes them.
The colleagues who **refuse** anything new are the ones at risk.
do: Pay about **eight hundred** for a robot programming certificate.
Ask to **shadow the integrator** when Hollins installs its first robot.
Pitch a **cobot palletiser** for the case-stacking job.
feel: **Calm**, almost **excited**, and aware most people won't feel that.
S1.quote: The guys who refuse to touch anything new are the ones I worry about.
fieldNote: He treats steady change as a **career ladder**, from operator to robot technician.
His progressive side shows in caring that colleagues like **Dev** aren't sacked.
He'd actively **push for automation** on the worst, most back-breaking task.

steps.text: Pay for a robot programming certificate, about eight hundred
Shadow the integrator when Hollins installs its first robot
Pitch a cobot palletiser for case stacking on line two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this needs a public plan: robot taxes, a basic income, free retraining for everyone. This isn't something one guy with a PLC certificate can fix. I'd join the union campaign and share it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my plan gets squeezed from both ends. By 2028 AI can probably write PLC code better than me, and by 2031 robots can do the hands-on fixing. So my safe spot is maybe the three years in between, installing and repairing robots while companies scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit Hollins in the first year and join one of the robot installers, the ones putting cells into every plant round here, because that's where the work would rush. I'd put more into savings, not the index fund, because markets would be wild. And I'd go to every union meeting about a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. For the first time it doesn't feel like I'm ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If thinking AI can write the robot programs by 2028, where does that leave your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin works in a call centre, so his job goes in 2028, three years before mine. I'd tell him to come in with me on the robot installs, because for a few years that's where the money is. After that, I don't know, and I'd tell him I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't fall apart, it shrinks. Instead of a career, I'd get a window, maybe three or four good years. I'd earn as much as I can in that window and save most of it.

say: This needs a **public plan**: robot taxes, basic income and free retraining.
One person with a **PLC certificate** can't fix this alone.
think: AI writes the **code** by 2028 and robots do the **fixing** by 2031.
My safe spot shrinks to about **three years** in between.
do: Quit Hollins in the first year to join a **robot installer**.
Move new money into **cash savings** rather than the index fund.
Attend every **union meeting** about a robot tax.
feel: **Anxious**, because for once he doesn't feel ahead.
S2.quote: Instead of a career, I'd get a window, maybe three or four good years.
fieldNote: Even this adaptive operator sees his **upgrade path** squeezed from both ends.
He'd **switch employer** fast to ride the installation rush.
He's honest with his cousin that he **doesn't know** what comes after.

steps.text: Leave Hollins to join a local robot installation firm
Shift new money from the index fund into cash
Attend union meetings pushing for a robot tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it fairly if we start now: retraining money, shorter working weeks, a share of robot profits for workers. I'd say it at work and online. I'd push the union to get Hollins to sign a training deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's better for me. Robots on the floor around 2034 gives me about eight years. I can be a robot technician for a good stretch and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the PLC course and the robot certificate in the next eighteen months. Then I'd move to an installer in 2028 when the rush starts. And I'd ask the union to get Hollins to pay for courses for everyone on the line, not just me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I've got a plan, so it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years make your controls plan work again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the index fund going, because there's time for it to grow. Maybe buy a small flat with my cousin, so we're not paying rent if work dries up later. I'd rather own four walls than have shares in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your money in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, the older guy on line one, would be close to retiring by 2034, so he might be fine. It's the people in their thirties now who'd get stuck. I'd want to drag a few of them onto the course with me.

I'd push for a **training deal** for everyone on the line.
think: About **eight years** before robots reach my floor gives me a real stretch.
I can work as a **robot technician** for years and save hard.
do: Finish the PLC and **robot certificates** within eighteen months.
Move to a **robot installer** in 2028 when demand rises.
Buy a **small flat** with my cousin to cut future costs.
S3.quote: I'd rather own four walls than have shares in 2035.
fieldNote: Five years turns his window back into a **career stretch**.
He'd convert savings into **property** as protection for later.

steps.text: Finish the PLC and robot programming certificates within eighteen months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so it's a test of whether our politics works. If we can't sort out retraining and a fair share in a decade, we deserve the mess. I'd say that online and probably get shouted at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's mostly good. I'd get maybe twelve years in robotics before robots fix themselves, and by then I'd be almost forty with a lot saved. I'd have time for one more switch after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same path but calmer: finish the courses, become the controls technician at Hollins, then look at robot work in about 2030. I'd keep the index fund growing. And I'd run a short lunch session for the older guys on using the AI app for fault codes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the decade change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to train, change jobs, and train again if I have to. I'd use the first half to get really good at robots and the second half to work out what's next. Maybe teaching it, maybe something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people use ten years as an excuse to do nothing, then 2039 is just 2028 with a delay. That's the political part that worries me. For me, personally, not much.

say: Ten years is a test of whether our **politics works**.
Failing to arrange **retraining** in a decade would be our own fault.
think: I'd get about **twelve years** in robotics before robots fix themselves.
I'd be nearly forty with **plenty saved** and time for another switch.
do: Become the **controls technician** at Hollins, then move into robot work around 2030.
Run **lunch sessions** teaching older colleagues the AI fault-code app.
S4.quote: If people use ten years as an excuse to do nothing, then 2039 is just 2028 with a delay.
fieldNote: His worry here is **political**, not personal.
He plans for **two career switches**, robotics first and something new later.
He'd use his skills to help **older colleagues** use AI tools.

steps.text: Become controls technician at Hollins, then move into robotics around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole plan becomes a three-year window. What would help is free robot and controls courses at the technical college, and some of the money companies save being paid back to workers, like a dividend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether people like me want the robots. A lot of us do, for the heavy jobs, as long as we're the ones who run them. Being for the robot and against the sack is not a contradiction.

headlineQuote: Being for the robot and against the sack is not a contradiction.

He's **calm** in slow worlds and sees steady disruption as a ladder up.
In AGI by 2028 his career shrinks to a **three-year window**, which makes him anxious.
He wants **robots for heavy jobs** with protection for colleagues and a share of savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his career plan shrinks to a three-year window.
